questions.question: At what frequency should rescue breaths be given during mouth to mouth resuscitation?
options: Four to six times per minute
Twenty to twenty-five times per minute
Twelve to sixteen times per minute
Thirty to forty times per minute
questions.explanation: The rescuer copies a normal resting breathing rhythm, which is twelve to sixteen breaths a minute; blowing far faster or slower does not ventilate the casualty properly.

questions.question: Why must the unconscious person's head be kept bent backwards throughout mouth to mouth resuscitation?
options: It stops blood from running into the stomach
It makes the chest easier to watch
It keeps the trachea open and unblocked
It takes the strain off the neck vertebrae
questions.explanation: With the head tilted back the airway stays clear, so the air you blow in actually reaches the lungs and can escape again.

questions.question: The casualty starts breathing normally again before the ambulance arrives. What should you do?
options: Leave the scene once other drivers are there
Sit the person upright and offer a warm drink
Keep monitoring the person until the ambulance comes
Continue rescue breaths at your own rhythm
questions.explanation: Breathing can stop again at any moment, so the casualty must be watched continuously until professional help takes over.

questions.question: At what rate should chest compressions be delivered when performing CPR?
options: At least 100 compressions per minute
At least 60 compressions per minute
About 40 compressions per minute
About 200 compressions per minute
questions.explanation: Only fast, hard compressions keep blood moving to the brain; a slower rhythm does not maintain circulation.

questions.question: How many chest compressions are given in a row before the two rescue breaths?
options: Five compressions
Thirty compressions
Fifteen compressions
Sixty compressions
questions.explanation: The recommended cycle for an unresponsive casualty with irregular breathing is thirty compressions followed by two rounds of mouth to mouth.

questions.question: Who is allowed to use an automatic external defibrillator (AED) in an emergency?
options: Anyone who is present at the scene
Only a doctor or a nurse
Only paramedics and police officers
Only someone with a first aid certificate
questions.explanation: AEDs are placed in public buildings precisely so that any bystander may use one when an emergency occurs.

questions.question: What has to be done to the patient's chest before the AED electrodes are attached?
options: It must be warmed up with a blanket
It must be dried of any sweat or moisture
It must be wiped over with a wet cloth
It must be covered with a thin dressing
questions.explanation: Moisture stops the sticky pads from sitting properly on the skin and can let the shock spread across the chest instead of through the heart.

questions.question: The patient regains consciousness and starts breathing while an AED is connected. What should you do?
options: Switch the AED off and remove the electrodes
Keep the AED on with the electrodes in place
Take the electrodes off but leave the AED on
Deliver one more shock before switching it off
questions.explanation: The heart can fall back into an irregular rhythm, and the device can only react to that if it is still running and connected.

questions.question: How should severe bleeding from a wound be stopped?
options: By tying a tight tourniquet around the limb
By pressing on the artery above the wound
By cooling the wound with ice or cold water
By pressing directly on the site of the wound
questions.explanation: Direct pressure on the wound itself is what closes the severed vessel, and the casualty can often apply it himself while you prepare a dressing.

questions.question: Blood is soaking through the bandage you have already applied to a wound. What should you do?
options: Take it off and press with your fingers
Loosen it so that the blood can drain away
Replace it with a clean, dry bandage
Put further bandages on top of the old one
questions.explanation: Taking the soaked bandage off releases the pressure that is holding the wound closed, so the bleeding gets worse instead of better.

questions.question: Above what speed at the moment of impact should you assume the people involved are probably injured?
options: 65 km/h
50 km/h
80 km/h
90 km/h
questions.explanation: A crash above this speed, like a rollover or someone thrown from the car, means serious head, neck or back injuries must be assumed even if nothing is visible.
